items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, with 83% being entirely unprompted by the developer. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases

items.title: What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
items.summary: Pathways is a single-controller distributed training system designed to coordinate large-scale model training across multiple accelerator groups by representing computations as a global dataflow graph. By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.

items.title: How to Choose Node.js Video Room Moderation: Muting or Kicking Participants (Presence First)
items.summary: A live game poll needs two different moderation actions. Mute should stop a participant from publishing audio while preserving their room membership, screen-share view, and ability to vote. Kick should revoke room membership, close every media path, and remove the participant from the presence roster. The important implementation detail is not the button. It is making presence derive from server-owned session state, so a disconnected or expelled player cannot remain visible as active. Short answer: default to mute for disruption and reserve kick for a participant who must lose access. Treat neither action as a client-side UI flag. The server must authorize publishes, votes, and reconnects against one monotonic membership record. That choice protects the live poll from the worst failure: showing a player as present after the system has stopped accepting their vote, or accepting a vote after the host believes the player is gone. WebRTC defines browser media primitives such as RTCPeerConnection, senders, receivers, and transceivers. It does not define your room membership protocol. items.title: I built an iOS app where your documents delete themselves
items.summary: We keep too many documents forever. Scans of contracts, tickets, IDs sent for a one-time procedure, a rental agreement from three years ago. Most of them only matter for a short time, and then they just sit in your phone, your cloud and your photo library, waiting to be leaked, lost or forgotten. So I built Fadely: an iOS app that works as a vault for temporary documents. You add a document, choose a date, and when that date arrives the document destroys itself. My brother-in-law flies constantly. His passport was buried among hundreds of downloads on his phone, and he always worried: what if it gets stolen? So in Fadely, docs get an expiry date. Then they're gone for good. 🔒 Most storage apps are built on one assumption: keep everything, forever. Fadely does the opposite. Every document has an expiry date from the moment you save it. You decide how long it should exist, and the app takes care of the rest. items.title: A 3-Stage Watermark Pipeline for Public Derivatives and Private Originals
items.summary: The operational constraint is ownership: a creator portfolio may display a transformed image to everyone, but the file being sold must never enter that public delivery path. Short answer: keep the original in private object storage, create a separate watermarked derivative for the portfolio, and issue a short-lived presigned link to the original only after a purchase has been verified. Persist the purchase-to-download authorization as its own record. This is a 3-stage system, not an image effect bolted onto an Express response. Upload establishes the private source of truth. Processing produces a replaceable public derivative. Fulfillment authorizes temporary access to the source. If those stages share a key, an ACL, or a cache namespace, the design has already spent most of its error budget. My first design assumption would be that a private bucket settles the question; tracing the emitted URLs corrects that assumption, because confidentiality depends on the entire delivery path rather than one storage setting. items.summary: I needed a signature pad for RapidKit Tools, a set of free browser-based tools I'm building. Most online signature tools upload the image to a server. The tool is built on react-signature-canvas, a React wrapper around signature_pad. Reading through the source taught me more than I expected, so here is what's actually going on under the hood. lineTo Connecting raw pointer coordinates with straight segments looks jagged. signature_pad buffers recent points, computes control points from them, and draws cubic Bézier curves. It also varies the stroke width with pointer velocity (faster movement gives a thinner line), and it rasterizes each curve by stepping along it and drawing small filled circles. The wrapper sizes the canvas bitmap to offsetWidth * devicePixelRatio and scales the 2D context to match, so strokes stay sharp on phone screens. items.title: What Really Happens When You Call a Function? Watching the Call Stack
items.summary: In this series, we use JSVisualizer, a free browser-based tool, to understand classic algorithms by watching them run. Last time we looked at conditionals. This time the topic is functions, and the star of the show is the Call Stack view. This program adds the squares of two numbers. 3 * 3 + 4 * 4 is 25. function square(x) { return x * x; } function sumOfSquares(x, y) { return square(x) + square(y); } let x = 10; let answer = sumOfSquares(3, 4); console.log(answer); console.log(x); What does the last line, console.log(x), print? People who've just met functions often wonder: x shows up in three places. It's a parameter (a variable that receives a value passed to a function) of square, a parameter of sumOfSquares, and the let x outside. Are these the same thing or different things? Where does execution go when you call a function, and how does it get back? Partway through square(x) + square(y), the program jumps into another function. How does it know where to pick up again? items.title: Node.js Cron Cleanup: 3 Stages for Expired User Sessions, Tokens, and Postgres Queues
items.summary: Short answer: use Node.js cron to request cleanup, not to perform it; claim expired sessions and tokens in bounded Postgres batches, make every delete and queue write idempotent, and expose a public webhook endpoint only as an authenticated trigger. For a weekly property-management digest, this favors predictable cost over instant cleanup while keeping the consumer free to retry. I've been paged for missed jobs and duplicate deliveries. The invariant from those incidents is plain: a schedule is evidence that a trigger was attempted, not evidence that the work completed exactly once. If the digest reads “active customers” while cleanup is racing it, an expired session can leak into the audience calculation or the same customer can be queued twice. So the design needs three durable stages: claim cleanup work, apply expiry, then enqueue the digest from the resulting active set. Cron starts the sequence. It doesn't own the sequence. Treat time as an input and progress as data. The Node.js process calculates a cutoff, creates a run identifier, and sends those values to the cleanup handler. items.title: What It Takes to Put Tab Autocomplete Inside Other Apps' Text Fields on macOS
items.summary: Autocomplete inside your own text view is a solved problem. You own the NSTextView, you know where the caret is, and you decide what Tab does. Autocomplete inside someone else's text field, in an app you did not write, is a different job. You don't own the text, the caret, or the Tab key. You borrow all three through macOS Accessibility, and each app lends them a little differently. We build DraftKey, a Mac app that suggests the rest of your sentence as you type and adds it when you press Tab. This post is about the plumbing behind that kind of feature. For the general mechanics I'm citing Apple's public documentation. For what we actually ran into, I'm citing our own public release notes: 52 tagged releases on GitHub, from 0.1.1 on September 20 to 0.1.62 on November 11, 2026. When I'm describing the macOS API surface in general rather than DraftKey's code, I'll say so. A Mac app can't read another app's text fields by default. items.summary: Short answer: For a Node.js queue service that must implement rate-limiting in message processing, use durable delivery with a shared rate budget, an idempotent expiry command, and a retry path that preserves the rental reservation record. That combination matters more than the queue brand. A rental hold that expires late can block inventory; one that expires twice can create a much harder reconciliation problem. Keep the command boring. The worker should claim an expiry job, wait for capacity, verify the hold is still eligible, and commit the state change in one transaction. Keep the queue responsible for delivery. Keep business truth in the property database. That boundary gives an operator somewhere reliable to start recovery when a worker disappears. In practice, implementing rate-limiting in Node.js means separating the local worker loop from the shared budget: a process-local counter can look correct in a test while several replicas exceed the upstream limit together. items.title: Object Storage API Economics 2026: 3 Tenant Checks for Node.js Browser Uploads

For a customer-support system, the storage bill is not the decisive number. The useful measure is the effective cost of keeping each tenant's attachments isolated, proving which object belongs to which ticket, and restoring a selected application snapshot without guessing what the browser did. A cheap write that creates an unreconcilable namespace is expensive. This architecture decision therefore treats the database as the ownership ledger and private object storage as the byte store. The browser gets narrow, temporary upload authority. It doesn't get authority to select a tenant prefix, declare an upload complete, or turn an object public. items.title: A/B Testing a Law Firm Site Without Flicker or SEO Trouble
items.summary: Law firm sites are a hard place to run A/B tests. Traffic is modest, the conversion that matters is a phone call, and the pages being tested are often the same charge pages that bring in most of the firm's search traffic. Add a client-side testing script that hides the page until it swaps in a variant, and you can hurt both the visitor experience and search performance while trying to improve conversions. This post covers a setup that avoids the two most common problems: the flicker of original content before a variant appears, and test configurations that confuse search engines. It is aimed at developers and technical marketers who maintain sites for criminal defense firms, though most of it applies to any small service business. Most client-side testing tools work by loading the original page, then running JavaScript that changes headings, buttons or layout for visitors in the variant group. If the script loads late, visitors briefly see the original before it changes. To hide this, many tools add an anti-flicker snippet that sets the page to invisible until the test script finishes. items.title: Rate-Limited Game Worker Drains: FIFO Windows and Idempotency-Key Recovery
items.summary: Draining a rate-limited game worker pool is a recovery problem before it is a queue-selection problem. A FIFO queue can suppress a duplicate for five minutes, but it cannot make a payment, inventory update, or match reward exactly once. My default is a standard queue with an idempotent consumer and a durable job key; use FIFO deduplication as a short-lived filter, not as the correctness boundary. Short answer: keep the queue replaceable, persist an idempotency key before side effects, and choose FIFO only when a five-minute duplicate window helps operational recovery. For a solo team, Infrai fits the narrow middle: its queue is available through one plain REST contract, and the same key can cover adjacent backend capabilities as the game grows. That breadth matters during a migration because the application can keep its own job schema while swapping the queue implementation behind a small adapter. items.title: Talking to an IBM i (AS/400) from .NET: data queues, COBOL and a live web page
items.summary: If you have ever heard "AS/400" and thought "that thing from the 80s", this article is for you. IBM i (the modern name of the AS/400) is still running payroll, banking and logistics in thousands of companies. Sooner or later, a .NET developer is asked to talk to it. By the end of this article you will know how to: get a free IBM i account and look around it; create a data queue (the IBM i message queue) and read it from .NET; call a COBOL program from C# and get its answer back; let that COBOL program publish a message that your .NET service consumes; see the whole thing in a small web page. Everything below was run for real against a free server. The code is a small open-source library plus a demo web app. IBM i / AS/400: a server with its own operating system. Same machine family, different names over the years. Library: roughly a schema or a folder. Objects live inside libraries (MYLIB/MYQUEUE). 5250 / green screen: the text terminal used to work on an IBM i. Data queue (*DTAQ): a message queue built into the system. items.title: I built a whole action game in one HTML file
items.summary: Samurai Vengeance is a side-on samurai action platformer with 1000 stages, ten bosses, a three-hit combo, a parry and a dash. The game itself lives in one file: index.html. It is about 650 KB and roughly 8,800 lines of plain JavaScript, CSS and markup, drawn on HTML canvas with no game engine and no build step. That is mostly true, and the "mostly" is part of this post. Here is how the pieces fit, and where the single-file idea stops. It was my first game, and one file meant there was nothing to configure. No bundler, no module graph, no asset pipeline. Open the file, change a line, reload. Deploying is uploading a static page to Netlify. It also suits the platform. The whole point of the game is that anyone can play it from a link, on a phone or a computer, without installing anything. A single page that starts as soon as it loads fits that. The page has three stacked full-screen canvases: bg for the parallax background, c for the action, and fg for weather and foreground. Splitting them lets each layer run at a different cost. items.summary: Autora: Victoria Lavarello Vidaurre Cuando se registra un equipo en un laboratorio, no basta con guardar su nombre. También interesa conocer dónde está, quién es responsable y si puede utilizarse. TechInventory organiza esa información mediante una aplicación con React, una API en Express y documentos JSON en Apache CouchDB. El proyecto tiene un alcance concreto: registrar, consultar, actualizar y eliminar equipos; buscar por sus datos principales; filtrar por estado y mostrar un resumen. La base elegida es CouchDB real. No se reemplaza por una colección en memoria para simplificar el alojamiento. Un equipo reúne datos que suelen consultarse juntos. Por eso el documento incluye código, nombre, categoría, ubicación, responsable, estado y notas. El identificador se obtiene del código: un equipo LT-001 utiliza asset:LT-001. Las cuentas de acceso se distinguen con type: user y no aparecen en el listado del inventario. Esta decisión tiene una consecuencia útil: dos altas concurrentes con el mismo código compiten por el mismo identificador. CouchDB acepta una y rechaza la otra. items.title: Node.js Healthtech Review — Record Served Vendor Attribution for Later Quality Comparison
items.summary: A healthtech access reviewer needs a record of which model vendor served each request, alongside evidence of what one credential can reach. A dashboard grouped by the configured default cannot establish actual attribution for later quality comparison. Keeping every prompt indefinitely would create a different problem: the evidence store would become another place the reviewer must inspect for sensitive access. TL;DR: Read routing configuration when the Node.js service starts, record the served vendor from each request's response metadata in your own metrics, and refresh the configuration snapshot after changes. Compare quality within stable evaluation cohorts before pinning a vendor. Keep that comparison running afterward. For the access review, retain a compact attribution ledger and a separate, deliberately sampled quality dataset. Count the labels. Start with a proposed review artifact: a credential inventory reference, the workloads authorized to use it, the routing configuration observed at deployment, and counts of requests attributed to each served vendor. items.title: Node.js Browser Direct Upload: Fixing Generated Image Object Storage CORS Errors
items.summary: A valid presigned PUT is not enough for a browser upload. The bucket must also accept the browser's preflight request, and a storage layer without self-service CORS configuration leaves that part outside your control. For a receipt-processing SaaS, send the generated image or original receipt through your Node.js backend and write it to private object storage there. It is the simplest reliable path, and it keeps the audit original away from a public URL. items.title: Node.js Rate-Limit Handling for API Queues: Failure Isolation and Backlog Monitoring
items.summary: For Node.js queue processing of rate-limited API calls, retry transient failures a finite number of times, move repeatedly failed work to a dead-letter queue, and watch the backlog before deciding to redrive. Short answer: for rate-limited API processing in Node.js, use a main queue, move repeatedly failed calls to a DLQ, monitor both backlog and dead-letter volume, and redrive only after the dependency has recovered. The point is not to make retries clever. It is to stop a bad payload or a temporary upstream cap from becoming the whole system's workload. items.title: Architecting Offline-First Invoicing Without a Backend Black Box
items.summary: Every freelancer has experienced the 'airplane mode panic.' You’re sitting in a coffee shop with spotty Wi-Fi, the client is ready to sign, and your SaaS-based invoicing tool is stuck on a spinning loading wheel, failing to authenticate against a remote server. It’s a failure of architectural philosophy: why should your ability to generate a PDF depend on a server halfway across the world? When we started building Vanza Invoices, we decided to stop treating the browser and mobile device as thin clients. We inverted the model. The device is the source of truth; the cloud is optional, or completely irrelevant. Most modern apps rely on a 'sync-everything' middleware that pipes data to a central database before reflecting it back to the UI. This introduces latency, subscription overhead, and catastrophic failure points when the connection drops. We moved to a local-first storage architecture utilizing IndexedDB, wrapped in a reactive persistence layer. By treating the local storage as the primary database, the app achieves sub-10ms read/write operations. When a user creates an invoice, the data lives exactly where it was typed—on the device. items.title: I built a Theme Studio where you plug a theme into a display and watch it stream in ⚡
items.summary: Hey everyone 👋 My portfolio has five themes: Classic, Terminal, Notebook, Midnight and Panorama. A dropdown would have been the easy way to switch between them. I wanted switching themes to feel like plugging a cable into a screen. So I built a Theme Studio. Pick a theme from the row of cards, and it slides in under the display Watch the display: it plays that theme's real page, live, and you can scroll it Drag the display or a card around, and the wires follow on a spring Hit Open: light races up the wires, a progress bar fills on the screen, and the theme opens Press Esc mid-send to pull the plug The connection isn't one line. It's a bundle of hairline strands, gold through orange, red and magenta to violet, pinched in the middle like a cable tie. Every strand is its own curve. Each one is a cubic bezier from a point on the card's edge to a point on the display's edge, so the bundle fans out at both ends. Light runs down it. Bands of brighter colour travel along the strands, and in dark mode they're blended additively so overlapping strands glow. It has weight. items.title: Four lessons from building a handwriting notes app for iPad
items.summary: I've been building GraphNotes, a notes app for iPad, iPhone Duo, and Mac where handwriting, PDF highlights and typed notes share one library. Two rules shaped most of its technical decisions: The ink is the note. The app reads your handwriting so it can search it, but it never swaps your strokes for its guess at what they say. Every thought keeps its way back. A note written beside a highlighted passage stays linked to that exact passage, and links point at permanent IDs, never at titles. It's built with SwiftUI (and UIKit where touch handling needs it), PencilKit, SQLite (libSQL through a fork of GRDB) and CloudKit's CKSyncEngine. Here are four things that took me longer to get right than I expected, in case they save you some time. It's tempting to spot new strokes by comparing drawing.strokes.count. Undo, redo and the vector eraser all break that. What works is diffing the strokes of two states by PKStrokePath.creationDate, the wall-clock time the pen touched down. items.title: Distributed Ray Tracer
items.summary: Hey HN, I'm Julius, I'm a backend engineer at Hatchet and created this demo to show off some of Hatchet's new features, primarily durable streams and serverless endpoints. Those, however, are just background details that made this significantly easier to scale. By distributing the rendering across many different nodes, orchestrated using Hatchet, it makes it possible to render quite high fidelity scenes fairly quickly. All of this would be possible on a single machine, but would be much slower without dedicated hardware (RT cores, etc). The renderer itself is using well-known ray tracing techniques, with no special considerations there. The renderer is a slightly modified version of https://github.com/ekzhang/rpt, with additional support for SDF scripting using https://docs.rs/fidget/latest/fidget/. SDFs have been popular in the demoscene community, though perhaps not super well known outside of that, and are capable of creating some fantastic looking scenes: https://www.shadertoy.com/view/ld3Gz2. Pick one, wire up the API, build some templates, and ship it. Quick disclosure: I founded DropInBlog and have been building blog software since 2015. Sooner or later, every one of them asked for a blog. The standard fix was WordPress on a subdomain with a custom theme built to match. It worked. It was also cumbersome. The result supported the long-standing idea that the centers of galaxies house supermassive black holes. However, scientists have since had some disagreements on whether the details and structure of the ring in the original publication were accurate. items.summary: A critical flaw in Apache HTTP Server's HTTP/2 module could allow unauthenticated attackers to remotely execute code and potentially take control of affected server processes. Tracked as CVE-2026-119618, the vulnerability affects Apache HTTP Server 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 when HTTP/2 is enabled and is fixed in version 2.4.71. The Hacker News reports: The vendor's assessment, published yesterday, also says "public research has demonstrated a reliable exploit" against a server in its default configuration with mod_http2 enabled. It does not name or link that research. Security company Wiz said later that day that no exploit was available and that no exploitation in the wild had been reported. HTTP/2 runs only where the Protocols directive turns it on, as the module documentation explains. The directive uses h2 for HTTP/2 over TLS and h2c for HTTP/2 over plain TCP. It can be set for the whole server or for a single virtual host, so admins should check the server-wide setting and every virtual host. items.title: What Changes With the A2UI 1.0 Release
items.summary: This article walks through what changed between A2UI 0.9 and A2UI 1.0, how generated UI works on 1.0, and why it is better, using one currency agent built on both versions. A Google ADK agent on Gemini looks up exchange rates and answers with A2UI cards and charts, rendered by a Next.js CopilotKit front end over AG-UI. https://github.com/xbill9/currency-claude-agui-a2ui1 On 0.9 the model wrote the UI as JSON, figures included. On 1.0 it writes one line and the server does the rest. A rate card for "Convert 100 USD to EUR" is 223 tokens of 0.9 JSON, 139 tokens of 1.0 Express, and 21 tokens as a 1.0 server-side macro call. A 90-day history chart is 1,060 tokens of 0.9 JSON and 21 as a macro call. Counted with the Gemini tokenizer, for the same components. A2UI is a protocol for agents that answer with UI. The agent sends a description of components (cards, text, buttons, charts) from a catalog the client implements, and the client renders them with its own native widgets. The agent never sends code, so the client decides what can run. items.title: F# for Beginners: Functional Programming on .NET
items.summary: F# is a functional-first language on .NET, made by Microsoft. If you know C#, you already know the ecosystem — the same libraries, the same runtime, the same tooling. What F# changes is how you write: less boilerplate, immutable data by default, and a type system that catches mistakes before your code runs. Many developers who try F# say their C# gets better afterwards, even if they never switch. A small example shows the difference: // average a list of numbers, safely let average numbers = match numbers with | [] -> None | xs -> Some (List.sum xs / float xs.Length) average [10.0; 20.0; 30.0] // Some 20.0 The Option type (Some or None) replaces null. Instead of a null reference crashing your program at runtime, the compiler forces you to handle the empty case. Pattern matching, pipelines (|>) and type inference mean F# programs are often half the length of the equivalent C# — and easier to read once you learn the idioms. F# is a good fit for backend services, data analysis, finance, and anywhere correctness matters. It is used in production for trading systems, web APIs (with Giraffe or Saturn), and data work. items.summary: Verifying CVE-2026-102870 remediation with package versions and build evidence A remediation ticket for CVE-2026-102870 should not close on a generic .NET update notice. Microsoft's advisory requires the affected Blazor WebAssembly debugger packages to move to fixed versions. The evidence needs to show which package version the project actually resolved. Microsoft rates CVE-2026-102870 High with CVSS 3.1 score 8.8. It is a CWE-94 code injection issue in the Blazor WebAssembly debugger. The affected package names are Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.Server and Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.DevServer. The vulnerable ranges are 10.0.0 through 10.0.13 and 11.0.0-preview.1 through 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148. Fixed versions are 10.0.14 and 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148. Begin with the project or branch that developers use to debug the application. Capture the target framework, direct package reference and resolved dependency version. A lockfile, restore log or generated SBOM can provide that record. Next, confirm the environment can actually load the fixed package. items.summary: I read a lot on a Kindle, and a lot of what I want to read only exists as a PDF. Some are clean exports with real text. Many are scanned books: 400 photos of pages, 180 MB, slightly crooked. You can send a PDF straight to a Kindle, but the result is bad. A PDF has fixed pages, so on a 6" screen the text is tiny and you can't make it bigger. What you want is an EPUB, which reflows to fit the screen and lets you change the font and text size, like a book bought from the store. The usual recipe takes four tools: one for OCR, Calibre to convert, something to shrink the images, then email or Amazon's app to send. items.summary: This article was created with the help of AI. The numbers come from my own site's Search Console and server logs. On October 8 I opened my own news site, promtime.net, on my phone and got Cloudflare's error 1015 instead of a page. My own rate-limiting rule had blocked me, and all I had done was read posts on it. The cause was a Next.js feature that exists to make the site feel fast. Two days later Search Console showed me the same feature from Googlebot's side. Between August 10 and October 22 Googlebot made 25,943 requests to the site, and Search Console filed 16,284 of them under "Other file type": not pages, not images, not scripts. When a scrolls into view, the Next.js router prefetches the page behind it. It requests the same URL with an _rsc parameter and an RSC: 1 header and gets back the React Server Components payload instead of HTML, so the click that follows feels instant. items.title: Reduced motion in Framer Motion: what I learned adding it to 150+ files
items.summary: Most sites handle reduced motion with one CSS rule. beUI's site has it too: @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { *, *::before, *::after { animation-duration: 0.01ms !important; transition-duration: 0.01ms !important; } } It's worth having, but on a Framer Motion site it isn't enough. Turn on "Reduce motion" with only this rule in place, and drawers still slide in, tabs still spring and counters still roll. That CSS only shortens CSS animations and transitions. Framer Motion works out each frame of a spring in JavaScript and writes the result to the element's style, so the media query never sees it. I build beUI, a library of animated React components, and more than 150 of its files now read the reduced motion setting. Here's what I learned doing that. null import { useReducedMotion } from "motion/react"; const reduce = useReducedMotion() ?? false; useReducedMotion() returns true when the setting is on. It returns null during server rendering, because the server can't know. The ?? false gives you a plain boolean, so you don't have to remember the third case everywhere. Reduced motion doesn't mean no animation. People turn the setting on because movement makes them dizzy or sick

items.title: Build a Sales Report API in ASP.NET Core with PDF, XLSX and CSV
items.summary: Sooner or later, most business apps need the same two things: a report someone can print, send or archive, and a spreadsheet with the same numbers that someone else can sort and filter. If you build them in two separate code paths, they drift apart. A total gets rounded differently, a column goes missing, a month filter behaves slightly differently. In this tutorial you build a small ASP.NET Core minimal API that generates a monthly sales report on the server and returns it as PDF, XLSX or CSV from one report definition. The report groups orders by customer, prints a subtotal per customer and a grand total, takes the month from the query string, marks the PDF as PDF/A-3b with one extra line, and saves its layout to JSON so you can load it back later. The report engine is sgcReports .NET, a headless engine with bands, expressions, data sources, pagination and PDF, XLSX, CSV and PNG export. You'll use the free Community package from nuget.org. items.title: My Mac windows kept landing on the wrong Space after every monitor swap, so I wrote a small app for it
items.summary: I use a MacBook with one external monitor at a time, and I swap between a few monitors during the week. Every time I plug a monitor back in, macOS brings the windows back to that screen, but not to the Space they were on. Chrome ends up on desktop 3, Slack on desktop 1, and I spend the first few minutes dragging things around. I wanted something that remembers, for each monitor, which Space every window belongs to. I couldn't find a tool that did exactly that, so I wrote LayoutKeeper, a small menu bar app. What it does: Saves a window layout per external monitor, keyed by the monitor's EDID, including which Space each window is on. When that monitor is plugged back in, it moves windows back to their saved Space and position. Tells Chrome windows apart by profile, so work and personal windows go back to the right places. Adds brightness keys for external monitors. What it doesn't do yet: when you unplug and go back to the built-in screen only, it doesn't restore a separate layout for that. There is an open issue for it (#2) and it's the next thing I want to build. It's free and open source (GPL-3.0), with builds for Apple Silicon and Intel: https://github.com/tumingke0/LayoutKeeper

items.title: Building a Private Classifier with Apple's On-Device Model and NLContextualEmbedding
items.summary: Apple's on-device model is a small language model that ships with macOS and iOS. It runs offline, costs nothing per call, and never sends your data anywhere. This article covers what it is good at, where it falls short, and how to build a classification engine from two pieces: NLContextualEmbedding and the Foundation Models framework. Size and context. The model has roughly 3 billion parameters. Its context window was about 4,096 tokens at launch, and that budget covers instructions, prompt and response together. Check the context size on your target OS version, because it can change between releases. A long document will not fit, so plan to chunk it. Speed. It runs on the Neural Engine and GPU, and generation is fast enough to feel interactive on Apple silicon. Time to first token is short, so short classification calls come back quickly. Throughput varies a lot with the chip and with the length of the output, so measure on your own hardware before quoting numbers. What it is good for: Classifying and tagging text. items.title: Tim Peters, Python User #2 and Prolific Contributor, Dies At 74
items.summary: Tim Peters, one of Python's earliest and most influential contributors, died on July 15 at age 74. Known as Python's second real user, Peters created the Zen of Python and Timsort sorting algorithm while contributing to numerous core components. He also served as a Python Software Foundation director from 2001 to 2014. Adafruit remembers Peters in a blog post: He's best known for the Zen of Python, PEP 20, still printed by typing import this. In 2002, he gave Python Timsort, the sorting algorithm he designed for lists, later adopted by Java and Android. He also polished the cyclic garbage collector and the pymalloc allocator, worked on the dict implementation, the float object, the math module and Karatsuba multiplication in longobject, and wrote the first version of doctest, plus difflib, pickletools and tabnanny. He was a director of the Python Software Foundation from 2001 to 2014. Before Python, he wrote compilers at Cray Research and speech-to-text software at Dragon Systems. The thread is full of recollections from core developers about his patient, detailed answers on the mailing lists, signed with his trademark . items.summary: A practical field guide for iOS developers building VPN and Network Extension apps with NEPacketTunnelProvider. Packet Tunnel Providers are hard to debug because they don't behave like a normal app. This post collects the setup, tools and habits that saved me the most time. I'd love to hear what has worked for you too. A packet tunnel runs as an app extension, which means: It's a separate process. Your host app and the extension have different lifecycles, and Xcode attaches to only one of them by default. The system controls its lifecycle. iOS launches and kills the extension, not you. It can be started, stopped or restarted without your app being in the foreground. It needs a real device. Here is how it is built, and a practical walkthrough for building your own Connect IQ app. This is part 1 of a series. Part 2 will be about watch faces. Garmin apps are written in Monkey C with the free Connect IQ SDK. The easiest editor is VS Code with Garmin's official Monkey C extension. You test in the bundled simulator, sideload a .prg file to your own watch over USB, and publish a signed .iq package through Garmin's web portal. If you know Java, JavaScript or Swift, your first app will run in the simulator in an evening. items.title: Power Grids On 5 Continents Pulse Every 60s. Scientists Think They Know Why
items.summary: "ScienceAlert is reporting that researchers may have finally determined why, for many years, power grids around the world have been pulsing every 60 seconds," writes longtime Slashdot reader fahrbot-bot. The likely culprit? Uninterruptible power supplies running routine battery checks. From the report: Every minute, some uninterruptible power supplies perform routine battery checks, creating small but measurable surges in electricity demand. And it's like clockwork. "Even benign control routines can become systemically relevant when many devices act coherently," writes a team led by physicist Dirk Witthaut of the University of Cologne, Germany, in a paper published in Nature Energy. "Unintended synchronization can generate recurrent and potentially amplified oscillatory behavior in large-scale cyber-physical energy systems." To figure it out, Witthaut and his colleagues analyzed high-resolution electricity measurements from buildings at the Forschungszentrum Julich research campus in Germany. In its heyday, the SS United States crushed the trans-Atlantic speed record, which it still holds. items.title: Handing over humanity (22 minute read)
items.summary: Some AI experts believe that once we achieve superintelligence, humans will be permanently disempowered, and we shall all be ruled by an AI god. This might not be such a desirable outcome, as humans have a natural desire for freedom. The arrangement will probably not work, as keeping power responsive to human needs has required checks developed over centuries, sustained by repeated feedback from the real world and correction, and there's no reason to keep that equilibrium stable once humans have surrendered all control. Humans have the ability now to steer the technology in a way that will not lead to a complete replacement of human judgment.

items.title: What objective is reasoning solving? (12 minute read)
items.summary: Reasoning is pathfinding in token space. There are many paths from the problem to a correct answer, and the model traverses each of them with each sample. A path is not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer - it's only in aggregate, over the distribution of paths, do we get a high probability of success. RL training directly raises the success probability. The gains credited to 'thinking longer' come from the search paid for during training rather than at inference.

items.title: Two Kinds of Test-Time Scaling (28 minute read)
items.summary: Test-time scaling trades compute for performance at test time. There are two types of test-time scaling: one allows researchers to trade more compute for more performance per task, but only up to the maximum quantity of per-task compute used during training; and the other lets researchers trade more compute for more performance per task, and lets them do so up to quantities of compute and performance that never occurred during training. Scaling methods that permit the latter change will have a larger impact than test-time scaling considered simply. This essay describes how this may impact the world.

They would be ushered one by one into a darkened room to sit facing an enormous TV. There would be a dish of sweets on a low bench in front of them but, in the reverential hush that descended, it was never entirely clear if it was acceptable to eat them. After a few moments, the screen would come to life. Rockstar would sometimes begin its presentation not with footage from its new game, but clips from classic movies. items.title: They Created a Cell That's Almost Alive. What to Do With It Now? (8 minute read)
items.summary: A SpudCell is an artificial cell created from lifeless ingredients that can grow, copy its DNA, divide in two, and start its cell cycle all over again. It is still far from a self-sustaining cell that any scientist could manufacture from prepared ingredients, but the technology could eventually make it easier to produce medicines, foods, and other items that could not otherwise be produced with ordinary biology. The researchers working on SpudCell hope that it will eventually be a platform for biotechnology that will allow a simple cell to be engineered in scores of useful ways. SpudCell could potentially be misused, so its researchers are taking security seriously from the start - its DNA and proteins are engineered so that it can only survive on an exotic diet of chemicals not found in nature.
